items.label: section_header
items.text: CALCULATIONS INVOLVING ONLY MASSES

items.label: text
items.text: Typical calculations will give you a mass of starting material and ask you to calculate how much product you are likely to obtain. You will also find examples done in reverse, where you are told the mass of the product and are asked to find out how much of the starting material you would need. In almost all the cases you will see at International GCSE you will be given the equation for the reaction. items.label: section_header
items.text: A PROBLEM INVOLVING HEATING CALCIUM CARBONATE

items.label: text
items.text: When calcium carbonate, CaCO3, is heated, calcium oxide is formed. Imagine you wanted to calculate the mass of calcium oxide produced by heating 25g of calcium carbonate (A: C = 12, O = 16, Ca = 40).

items.label: formula
items.text: C a C O _ { 3 } \rightarrow C a O + C O _ { 2 }

items.label: text
items.text: The method we will use has three steps:

items.label: list_item
items.text: Step 1: Calculate the number of moles using the mass that you have been given.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Step 2: Use the chemical equation to work out the number of moles of the substance you are interested in.

items.label: text
items.text: Step 3: Convert the number of moles to a mass.

items.label: text
items.text: In this reaction we have 25 g of CaCO₃ and the number of moles can be calculated as:

items.label: formula
items.text: b u n r o f m o l e = \frac { \ m a s s } { \ m a s s \, o f \, 1 \, m o l e } = \frac { 2 5 } { 1 0 0 } = 0 . 2 5 \, m o l

items.label: text
items.text: The chemical equation for this reaction is

items.label: formula
items.text: C a C O _ { 3 } \rightarrow C a O + C O _ { 2 }

items.label: text
items.text: We can see from the equation that 1mole of CaCO₃ will decompose to produce 1 mole of CaO. In other words, the equation is telling us that if we start with a certain number of moles of CaCO₃ we will obtain the same number of moles of CaO at the end.

items.label: text
items.text: Therefore, we can deduce that 0.25 mol CaCO3 will decompose to produce 0.25 mol CaO. Now that we know the number of moles of CaO (M = 56) we can convert this to a mass:

items.label: text
items.text: mass = number of moles × mass of 1 mole

items.label: formula
items.text: \ m a s s = 0 . 2 5 \times 5 6 = 1 4 g

items.label: text
items.text: Therefore, the reaction will produce 14 g of calcium oxide.
